questions.q: Why is it extremely important to wrap each parameter and the entire expression in parentheses ((a) * (b)) when creating a parameterized macro #define MULTIPLY(a, b) a * b?
questions.hint: Think about how the macro will expand when passing expressions with addition operations, such as MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4).
options: To avoid violating operator precedence when passing complex expressions as arguments
To allocate dynamic memory for the evaluation result
To force the compiler to turn the macro into an inline function
This is a C standard syntax requirement; without parentheses the code will not compile
explanations: Correct! Due to text substitution 'as is', the expression `MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3 + 4)` will expand to `1 + 2 * 3 + 4 = 11` instead of the expected `(1 + 2) * (3 + 4) = 21`. Wrapping in parentheses guarantees the correct mathematical order of operations.
Incorrect. The preprocessor only performs text substitution and does not allocate memory.
Incorrect. Parentheses do not turn a macro into a function.
Incorrect. Code without parentheses will compile, but will lead to logical errors due to operator precedence.

questions.q: What is the scope of a macro declared via #define BUFFER_SIZE 1024 inside a function body?
questions.hint: Does the preprocessor know about curly braces {} and function blocks in C?
options: From the point of declaration to the end of the translation unit file (or until the #undef directive) — the preprocessor ignores function boundaries
Limited to the {} block of the function inside which the macro was declared
The same as that of a regular local variable on the stack
explanations: Correct! The preprocessor works BEFORE the compilation phase and treats code as plain text. It knows nothing about functions or `{}` blocks. The macro is available everywhere from its point of declaration to the end of the file (or until `#undef`).
Incorrect. The preprocessor does not respect C code block boundaries.
Incorrect. Macros do not have local variable scope concepts.

questions.q: Which preprocessor directive is used to undefine (remove) a previously created macro?
questions.hint: The directive name is formed by adding the prefix un- to the word define.
options: #undef
#delete
#remove
#clear
explanations: Correct! The `#undef MACRO_NAME` directive resets a macro definition. After it, the name is no longer substituted by the preprocessor.
Incorrect. The `#delete` directive does not exist in C.
Incorrect. The `#remove` directive is absent.
Incorrect. The `#clear` directive is not part of the C standard.

questions.q: Which standard macro variable contains the current line number of the C source file during compilation?
questions.hint: The name contains the word LINE enclosed in double underscores.
options: __LINE__
__FILE__
__ROW__
__LINE_NUM__
__STDC_LINE__
explanations: Correct! The `__LINE__` macro is automatically replaced by the compiler with the current line number in the source file (an integer). It is often used together with `__FILE__` for error logging.
Incorrect. `__FILE__` contains the current file name as a string.
Incorrect. The `__ROW__` macro does not exist.
Incorrect. The name `__LINE_NUM__` is not standard.
Incorrect. Fictional macro name.

questions.q: What identifier is used in a parameterized macro with a variable number of arguments (e.g., #define LOG(fmt, ...)) to insert the passed argument list?
questions.hint: The name starts with double underscores and contains the words VA_ARGS.
options: __VA_ARGS__
__ARGS__
__VAR_ARGS__
explanations: Correct! Starting from C99, if a macro is declared with an ellipsis `...`, all additional passed arguments are substituted via the special identifier `__VA_ARGS__`.
Incorrect. The identifier `__ARGS__` does not exist.
Incorrect. The correct name is `__VA_ARGS__`.
Incorrect. The ellipsis `...` is used in the declaration, not in the macro body.

questions.q: Which character at the end of a line is used to continue a multi-line #define macro definition onto a new line?
questions.hint: This same character is used for escaping special characters.
options: Backslash \
Forward slash /
Double ampersand &&
Semicolon ;
explanations: Correct! Since a `#define` macro ends with a newline character, continuation to the next line is done using the backslash `\` (Line continuation character) at the very end of the line.
Incorrect. Forward slash is used for comments and division.
Incorrect. `&&` is a logical AND operator.
Incorrect. Semicolon in the preprocessor becomes part of the substituted text.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the constant #define LIMIT 10 and const int limit = 10;?
questions.hint: Does #define participate in compiler type checking?
options: #define performs text substitution without type checking, while const creates a real typed variable in memory
#define allocates memory on the heap, while const allocates on the stack
A const variable cannot be used in expressions, whereas #define can
There is absolutely no difference between them
explanations: Correct! `#define` works at the preprocessing stage and has no data type (the compiler simply sees the number `10`). A `const int` variable is checked by the compiler for type and has a real address in memory.
Incorrect. `#define` does not allocate memory at all.
Incorrect. `const` constants can be freely used in any expressions.
Incorrect. The difference is fundamental at the preprocessing and compilation stages.

questions.topic: Syntax — Space in Function-like Macro Declarations
questions.q: What will happen if a space is placed between the name of a parameterized macro and the opening parenthesis in its declaration: #define FOO (x) ((x) + 1)?
questions.hint: Will the macro turn into an object-like constant instead of a function-like macro with a parameter?
options: The preprocessor will create an object-like macro FOO with the value "(x) ((x) + 1)" instead of a function-like macro
The space will be automatically ignored by the preprocessor
A compilation error will occur
The macro will automatically be converted into an inline function
explanations: Correct! In C preprocessor syntax, a function-like macro requires the parenthesis to follow IMMEDIATELY after the name: `#define FOO(x)`. If a space is inserted, `FOO` becomes a regular object-like macro replacing text with `(x) ((x) + 1)`.
Incorrect. The space here fundamentally changes the macro type.
Incorrect. This is valid C code, so the preprocessor will not issue an error.
Incorrect. No function will be created.

questions.q: Which preprocessor directive allows checking if a macro with a specific name has been previously defined?
questions.hint: The directive name combines the words if and defined.
options: #ifdef (or #if defined(...))
#ifexist
#isdefined
#check
explanations: Correct! The `#ifdef MACRO` or `#if defined(MACRO)` directives check for the existence of a macro, regardless of what value is assigned to it.
Incorrect. The `#ifexist` directive does not exist in the C standard.
Incorrect. The `#isdefined` directive does not exist.
Incorrect. `#check` is not a C preprocessor directive.

questions.q: What will happen if an attempt is made to redefine a macro with a different value #define VAL 100 and below #define VAL 200 without a prior #undef VAL?
questions.hint: Will the compiler stop building or issue a warning?
options: The compiler will issue a warning about redefinition, and the macro will receive the new value 200
The program will not compile due to a fatal error
The new value will be ignored, keeping VAL == 100
Both values will merge into an array
explanations: Correct! Redefining a macro with different content is not strictly forbidden, but the compiler will issue a `macro redefinition` warning and overwrite the macro with the new value `200`.
Incorrect. This is a warning, not a critical error.
Incorrect. Priority is given to the latest declaration.
Incorrect. Arrays are not created in preprocessor macros this way.

questions.topic: Preprocessor vs Typedef — Type Replacement via #define
questions.q: What is the pitfall of using the macro #define INT_PTR int* when declaring multiple variables separated by commas INT_PTR a, b;?
questions.hint: How will text substitution of 'int*' affect the asterisk before the second variable name?
options: Variable a will become an int* pointer, while variable b will be a regular int
Both variables a and b will become int* pointers
A syntax compilation error will occur
Variable a will become int, while b will be an int* pointer
explanations: Correct! Because the preprocessor simply substitutes text, the line expands to `int* a, b;`. In C, the asterisk applies only to the name of the specific variable, so `a` will be of type `int*`, and `b` of type `int`. To correctly declare types, `typedef int* INT_PTR;` should be used.
Incorrect. Text substitution does not propagate `*` to variable `b`.
Incorrect. The code compiles completely, but variable `b`'s type will be unexpected.
Incorrect. The asterisk will attach to variable `a`.

questions.topic: Preprocessor — Repeated Evaluation in Ternary Operator
questions.q: What will be the values of variable res and variable a after executing the code int a = 5, b = 2; int res = MAX(a++, b); given the macro #define MAX(x, y) ((x) > (y) ? (x) : (y))?
questions.hint: How many times will variable a be substituted into the ternary operator and where will the increment execute?
options: res == 6, and variable a will equal 7 (due to two increments)
res == 5, and variable a will equal 6
res == 5, and variable a will equal 7
res == 6, and variable a will equal 6
explanations: Correct! The expression expands into `((a++) > (b) ? (a++) : (b))`. First, the condition `5 > 2` is evaluated (true, `a` becomes 6). Then the true branch `a++` executes (returns current 6 and increments `a` to 7). As a result, `res == 6` and `a == 7`.
Incorrect. The condition is true, so the `(a++)` branch executes a second time.
Incorrect. The second evaluation returns the value of `a` before the second increment (which is 6).
Incorrect. Repeated evaluation will perform the increment again.

questions.q: Why is a two-level wrapper used when turning the value of another macro into a string (e.g., #define STR_HELPER(x) #x and #define STR(x) STR_HELPER(x))?
questions.hint: Do macros inside the # operator expand directly?
options: So that the argument macro first expands into its value, and only then turns into a string
To automatically strip spaces from the created string
To force the preprocessor to allocate memory on the heap
This is a specific requirement for working with Unicode
explanations: Correct! The `#` operator suppresses macro expansion of arguments. Calling `STR_HELPER(VERSION)` yields the string `"VERSION"`. The intermediate macro `STR(VERSION)` first expands `VERSION` into its value (e.g., `1.0`), and then passes it to `STR_HELPER`, producing `"1.0"`.
Incorrect. The preprocessor does not remove spaces from strings.
Incorrect. The preprocessor works only with text during build time.
Incorrect. This is a general rule of macro expansion in ANSI C.

questions.q: What do the standard predefined macros __DATE__ and __TIME__ contain?
questions.hint: At what moment are the values of these macros fixed?
options: String literals with the date and time of file compilation
Current date and time at the moment of program invocation in seconds (time_t)
Runtime of the current process since startup
Time of last file modification on disk
explanations: Correct! The `__DATE__` (format `"Mmm dd yyyy"`) and `__TIME__` (format `"hh:mm:ss"`) macros are substituted by the compiler as string literals fixing the exact build moment of the module.
Incorrect. At runtime, these values do not change or update.
Incorrect. To measure execution time, functions from `<time.h>` are used.
Incorrect. File modification time is tracked by the build system (Make/CMake), not these macros.

questions.q: What will happen if a macro refers to its own name inside its definition (e.g., #define A (A + 1))?
questions.hint: Will the preprocessor enter an infinite expansion loop?
options: The preprocessor replaces A with (A + 1) and suppresses re-expansion of A, preventing looping
The preprocessor will hang due to infinite recursion
A fatal compilation error 'Recursive macro detected' will occur
The identifier A will automatically reset to 0
explanations: Correct! The C standard forbids recursive macro expansion: during re-scanning of substituted text, the macro name `A` is disabled, preventing infinite replacement.
Incorrect. Infinite looping does not occur thanks to C standard re-scanning rules.
Incorrect. No compilation error occurs.
Incorrect. The name `A` remains in text 'as is'.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the preprocessor directive #line 100 "custom.c"?
questions.hint: How does this affect compiler error output and __LINE__ / __FILE__ macros?
options: To forcibly change the values of __LINE__ and __FILE__ macros for subsequent lines of code
To jump to line 100 of the file during program execution
To limit the maximum number of lines in a file
To include an external file starting from line 100
explanations: Correct! The `#line` directive changes compiler internal counters: current line becomes 100, and file name becomes `"custom.c"`. Code generators (yacc/bison) often use this so compiler errors point back to the source DSL file.
Incorrect. The directive operates during compilation, not runtime.
Incorrect. File length limits are not set by the directive.
Incorrect. To include files, `#include` is used.

questions.q: How will the C compiler process two string literals written with a space, for example #define MSG "Hello, " "World!"?
questions.hint: Is a string addition operator needed in C?
options: Automatically merge them into a single string literal "Hello, World!"
Issue a compilation error because the + operator is missing
Create an array of two separate strings
Ignore the second literal
explanations: Correct! In C, adjacent string literals separated only by whitespace or newlines are automatically concatenated by the translator into a single string during text analysis phases.
Incorrect. C has no `+` operator for strings.
Incorrect. A single string literal is created.
Incorrect. Both parts of the string will be preserved.

questions.q: Is __func__ (C99) a preprocessor macro?
questions.hint: Can the presence of __func__ be checked via #ifdef __func__?
options: No, __func__ is an implicit local static variable created by the compiler inside every function
Yes, it is a regular preprocessor macro similar to __LINE__
Yes, it is a built-in macro available only in header files
No, it is a keyword for declaring functions
explanations: Correct! According to C99, `__func__` is not a preprocessor macro, but an implicitly declared array `static const char __func__[] = "function-name";` at the beginning of the function body. Therefore `#ifdef __func__` will not work.
Incorrect. Unlike `__FILE__` and `__LINE__`, the preprocessor knows nothing about `__func__`.
Incorrect. It is declared by the compiler during function syntax parsing.
Incorrect. It is the name of a built-in local array.

questions.topic: C23 / GNU Standard — Deleting Trailing Comma (__VA_OPT__)
questions.q: What problem does the __VA_OPT__(,) macro in C23 standard (or GNU extension , ## __VA_ARGS__) solve?
questions.hint: What happens to the comma before __VA_ARGS__ if the user calls a variadic macro without additional arguments?
options: Safely deletes the trailing comma if the additional argument list __VA_ARGS__ is empty
Automatically casts arguments to const char* type
Counts the number of passed arguments
Creates a variadic array on the heap
explanations: Correct! Calling macro `#define LOG(fmt, ...)` without arguments expanded `printf(fmt, __VA_ARGS__)` into `printf("test", )` with an extra comma. The `__VA_OPT__(,)` construct inserts a comma only if `__VA_ARGS__` is non-empty.
Incorrect. The macro does not perform type conversions.
Incorrect. Other macro tricks are used to count arguments.
Incorrect. Heap memory work is not performed.

questions.q: What will be the value of macro UNKNOWN_MACRO in conditional directive #if UNKNOWN_MACRO == 0 if it was not previously declared via #define?
questions.hint: How does the preprocessor handle unknown identifiers inside an #if expression?
options: The preprocessor will replace the unknown identifier with 0, and the condition will become true
A fatal preprocessor error 'Undefined macro' will occur
The condition is automatically deemed false
The preprocessor will replace it with the value -1
explanations: Correct! In `#if` and `#elif` directive expressions, any remaining unreplaced identifiers (except `defined`) are automatically replaced by the preprocessor with the integer `0`.
Incorrect. Undeclared macros in `#if` do not cause build abort.
Incorrect. Since it becomes 0, expression `0 == 0` yields 1 (true).
Incorrect. Default value is always 0.

questions.topic: Function-like Macros — Comparison with Inline Functions
questions.q: What is the main advantage of a static inline function over a #define function-like macro when implementing logic inside functions?
questions.hint: Does the preprocessor check argument types, unlike the compiler?
options: Inline functions provide strict argument type checking and are convenient for debugging (gdb), while maintaining direct inlining speed
Inline functions never increase final executable file size
Inline functions can be called before main function execution
Inline functions are automatically compiled for graphics card (GPU)
explanations: Correct! A `static inline` function combines body substitution speed (without call overhead) with strict compiler argument type checking and proper debugger visibility.
Incorrect. Like macros, excessive inlining of large functions increases binary size.
Incorrect. Calling inline functions follows standard control flow rules.
Incorrect. Unrelated to GPU subsystems.

questions.q: What will happen if a macro called inside a function expands into a return -1; instruction?
questions.hint: Where does the return statement belong during macro text substitution?
options: An immediate return will occur from the function in whose body the macro was called
The return statement will return a value from the macro itself without terminating the calling function
A compilation error 'illegal return in macro' will occur
The value -1 will be written to global variable errno
explanations: Correct! The preprocessor substitutes `return -1;` directly into the code of the outer function. Executing this line will terminate the outer function and return `-1`.
Incorrect. Macros do not create their own stack frame or function boundary.
Incorrect. Syntactically completely correct C code.
Incorrect. The `return` statement exits function, rather than setting `errno`.

questions.topic: Optimization — Disabling Functions in Release via #define
questions.q: How to correctly disable a debug function log_debug(...) via #define in a release build so that the compiler generates no call code?
questions.hint: What replaces a variadic macro call in C so that it turns into a 'noop' expression?
options: #define log_debug(...) ((void)0)
#define log_debug(...) NULL
#define log_debug(...) return 0
#define log_debug(...) break
explanations: Correct! The notation `((void)0)` represents a safe no-op expression. It fits syntactically with a trailing semicolon `;` anywhere in a function and is completely removed by the optimizer.
Incorrect. Using `NULL` without assignment will trigger compiler warnings.
Incorrect. This will terminate the calling function upon logging attempt.
Incorrect. `break` outside loop or `switch` will cause a compilation error.

questions.topic: Debugging — Function Wrapping with Metadata Passing
questions.q: Why is function void* custom_malloc(size_t sz, const char* file, int line) often wrapped with macro #define malloc(sz) custom_malloc(sz, __FILE__, __LINE__)?
questions.hint: How does the debug function learn where in user code memory was allocated?
options: To implicitly pass file name and call line number to the debug function for tracking memory leaks
To speed up memory allocation via precompilation
To make function call thread-safe
To forcibly allocate memory on stack instead of heap
explanations: Correct! At call site `malloc(100)`, the macro substitutes `__FILE__` and `__LINE__`, allowing memory profiler to record exactly which line of which file requested memory.
Incorrect. Allocation speed is determined by `malloc` algorithm.
Incorrect. Thread safety is ensured by mutexes/atomics, not macros.
Incorrect. Function continues allocating memory on heap.

questions.topic: GNU C Extensions — Block Expression ({ ... }) in Macros
questions.q: Why is the ({ ... }) construct (Statement Expression) used in GCC/Clang extensions when creating safe function-like macros?
questions.hint: How to declare a temporary local variable and force the macro to 'return' a result?
options: To declare local variables inside a macro and return the value of the last expression, avoiding repeated evaluation of arguments
To execute macro code in a separate background thread
To automatically turn macro into assembly insertion
To call a base class method
explanations: Correct! The `({ ... })` construct allows putting a compound block with local variables inside a macro, with the value of the last expression inside the block becoming the 'return value' of the macro.
Incorrect. No multithreading is created by this construct.
Incorrect. `__asm__` is used for assembly insertions.
Incorrect. There are no classes or inheritance in C.

questions.q: What is the idea behind applying the X-Macros idiom when generating functions or data tables in C?
questions.hint: How to avoid duplicating lists (enum, strings, handler functions) in different parts of a program?
options: The list of items is stored in a single macro, which is redefined and expanded multiple times to generate enums, string arrays, and functions
Function code is automatically parallelized across all CPU cores
All project functions are merged into one huge file using preprocessor
Used to protect source code from decompilation
explanations: Correct! The X-Macros pattern allows describing data once (as a list of lists), and then substituting different definitions of macro `X(...)` to automatically generate enums, string mappings, and function switch cases.
Incorrect. This is a preprocessor code generation pattern, not parallelization.
Incorrect. Project file structure does not change.
Incorrect. X-Macros is not code obfuscation or anti-tamper.

questions.topic: Generic Programming — typeof Keyword in Macros
questions.q: Why is typeof (or __typeof__) keyword used in safe function-like macros (e.g., minimum calculation MIN(a, b))?
questions.hint: How to preserve argument type when creating temporary local variables inside a macro?
options: To determine argument type and create local variables of same type, preventing repeated evaluation of side effects
To find exact data type size in bytes at runtime
To forcibly cast argument to void* type
To check if variable is a structure or pointer
explanations: Correct! Writing `typeof(a) _a = (a);` creates local variable `_a` of the same type as parameter `a`. This evaluates `a` exactly once, avoiding issues with `MIN(i++, j++)`.
Incorrect. `sizeof` is used to get memory size.
Incorrect. Casting to `void*` is done via `(void*)` syntax.
Incorrect. `typeof` does not inspect structures.

questions.topic: Working with Structures — offsetof Macro from <stddef.h>
questions.q: What does standard offsetof(type, member) macro calculate when manipulating structure fields inside functions?
questions.hint: How to find how many bytes offset from structure start a specific field occupies?
options: Offset of field member in bytes relative to start of structure type
Total size of structure type in bytes
Pointer to first field of structure
Number of fields contained in structure type
explanations: Correct! The `offsetof` macro returns a `size_t` value — the byte offset of field `member` from the start of structure `type`. Frequently used in low-level serialization or `container_of`.
Incorrect. Total structure size is computed by `sizeof(type)`.
Incorrect. That would cast structure address.
Incorrect. `offsetof` does not count field numbers.

questions.q: Why is replacing system functions like #define strdup _strdup often found in cross-platform code?
questions.hint: Do names of some standard functions differ in MSVC (Windows) and GCC (POSIX) compilers?
options: To ensure cross-platform building by adapting function names to specifics of a particular compiler/OS
To multiply strdup call execution speed
To forbid heap memory allocation
To make function calls completely hidden from system debugger
explanations: Correct! The MSVC compiler requires using POSIX functions with an underscore (e.g. `_strdup` instead of `strdup`). Using `#define`, developers maintain unified code syntax across all OSes.
Incorrect. The macro changes only called symbol name, without changing implementation.
Incorrect. Memory will still be allocated on heap.
Incorrect. Debugger sees final symbol `_strdup`.

questions.q: What problem can arise if a macro declares variable tmp inside block do { int tmp = ...; } while(0), and a variable with the same name already exists in the function?
questions.hint: Which variable will be hidden (shadowed) in the inner scope block?
options: Macro local variable will shadow outer variable tmp inside macro block, which can lead to logical error during interaction
A compilation error 'Duplicate symbol error' will occur
Outer variable tmp from calling function will automatically reset to zero
Program will crash with Segmentation Fault
explanations: Correct! New block `{}` creates its own scope. Inner `int tmp` hides outer `tmp`. If macro tries to read outer `tmp` (e.g., `a = tmp`), it reads its own newly created variable!
Incorrect. Declaring variable in inner block with same name is syntactically allowed in C.
Incorrect. Outer variable retains its value, but becomes inaccessible inside macro block.
Incorrect. No memory access errors occur here.
